lessonTitle: Air-Conditioning Processes: Cooling Coils, Mixing and Evaporative Cooling

blocks.text: The air handler of a hospital ward takes in 2 kg of air per second at 30 °C and a clammy 68% relative humidity and must deliver it at 14 °C. Cooling alone would leave the air at nearly 100% humidity, and the ward would feel like a cave. The coil therefore has to cool the air below its dew point so that water condenses out, which means the coil duty has two parts: removing sensible heat and removing latent heat.

blocks.markdown: Air-conditioning processes are steady-flow processes on moist air, analysed with a mass balance on dry air, a mass balance on water and an energy balance. Dry-air mass flow $\dot m_a$ is constant through every process, and enthalpies are per kg of dry air. The processes in this unit are **cooling with dehumidification**, **adiabatic mixing of two streams** and **evaporative cooling**.

blocks.title: Cooling with dehumidification
blocks.text: The air is cooled below its dew point by a cold coil. Water vapour condenses on the coil, so the humidity ratio falls from $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$ and the air leaves nearly saturated at the coil-surface temperature. The condensate leaves as liquid at about the exit temperature, with enthalpy $h_f$.

blocks.caption: $\dot m_w$ is the condensate rate (kg/s); $\dot Q_{coil}$ is the heat removed (kW); enthalpies in kJ/kg dry air and $h_f$ the enthalpy of liquid water leaving the coil (kJ/kg).

blocks.title: Cooling load with dehumidification
blocks.prompt: Air flows at $\dot m_a = 2.0$ kg/s dry air through a cooling coil. Inlet: 30 °C with $\omega_1 = 0.0182$. Exit: 14 °C with $\omega_2 = 0.0099$ (nearly saturated). Condensate leaves at about 14 °C with $h_f \approx 58.8$ kJ/kg. Find the condensate rate and the cooling load. Use $h = 1.005\,T + \omega(2501 + 1.82\,T)$.

steps.text: Condensate rate from the water balance.
Energy balance with the condensate enthalpy.

blocks.answer: Condensate = 0.0166 kg/s (about 60 kg/h); cooling load = 74.2 kW. The condensate term is only about 1% of the load but must not be forgotten.

blocks.title: Adiabatic mixing of two streams
blocks.text: Two moist-air streams (1 and 2) mix with no heat transfer and no work. Conservation of dry air, water and energy gives mass-flow-weighted averages for $\omega$ and $h$. On the psychrometric chart the mixed state lies on the straight line joining states 1 and 2, closer to the stream with the larger dry-air mass flow.

blocks.latex: \dot m_{a3} = \dot m_{a1} + \dot m_{a2} \qquad \omega_3 = \frac{\dot m_{a1}\omega_1 + \dot m_{a2}\omega_2}{\dot m_{a3}} \qquad h_3 = \frac{\dot m_{a1}h_1 + \dot m_{a2}h_2}{\dot m_{a3}}
blocks.caption: Weights are dry-air mass flow rates. Mixed dry-bulb temperature follows from $h_3$ and $\omega_3$ (and is approximately the mass-weighted average of the temperatures).

blocks.title: Mixing outdoor air with return air
blocks.prompt: In winter, 1.0 kg/s of outdoor air at 5 °C ($\omega = 0.0030$) mixes with 3.0 kg/s of return air at 24 °C ($\omega = 0.0090$). Find the humidity ratio, enthalpy and temperature of the mixture.
blocks.answer: Mixture: ω = 0.0075, h = 38.4 kJ/kg dry air, T ≈ 19.3 °C. The mass-weighted temperature average (19.25 °C) is a good approximation.

blocks.markdown: **Evaporative cooling.** Water is sprayed into a stream of dry air, evaporating by drawing its latent heat from the air itself. With no heat transfer to the surroundings the energy balance shows that the enthalpy of the air is almost unchanged (the small enthalpy of the added liquid water is negligible), so the process follows a line of constant enthalpy, which is also very close to a line of constant wet-bulb temperature. The dry-bulb temperature falls and the humidity ratio rises. The lowest temperature achievable is the **adiabatic saturation** (wet-bulb) temperature, at which the air leaves saturated.

blocks.caption: The water added equals the increase in humidity ratio times the dry-air flow (kg/s). The exit state of an ideal cooler is saturated, $\varphi_2 = 100\%$.

blocks.title: Water added by an evaporative cooler
blocks.prompt: Dry air at 35 °C with $\omega_1 = 0.0100$ flows at 1.5 kg/s dry air through an ideal evaporative cooler and leaves saturated at 21 °C with $\omega_2 = 0.0156$. Check that the enthalpy is nearly constant and find the water added.

steps.text: The two values agree within about 0.2%, confirming the constant-enthalpy (adiabatic saturation) process.

blocks.answer: Water added = 0.0084 kg/s (30.2 kg/h). The air is cooled by 14 K, entirely by evaporation, with no refrigeration plant.

blocks.title: Sensible and latent loads
blocks.text: The total cooling load is the sum of a **sensible** part (cooling the dry air and vapour) and a **latent** part (condensing water vapour). In humid climates the latent part can be 30% or more of the load, so a coil must be sized for both.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Use dry-air mass flow, not moist-air mass flow, in every balance. In mixing, weight $\omega$ and $h$ by dry-air mass flow rates, not by volume flows (the densities differ if temperatures differ). An evaporative cooler cannot cool below the wet-bulb temperature, which is why it works poorly in humid air.

points: Cooling with dehumidification: $\dot Q = \dot m_a[(h_1 - h_2) - (\omega_1-\omega_2)h_f]$ with condensate $\dot m_a(\omega_1 - \omega_2)$.
Adiabatic mixing: $\omega$ and $h$ are dry-air-flow-weighted averages; the mixture lies on the straight line between the two states.
Evaporative cooling is at constant $h$, with water added $\dot m_a(\omega_2 - \omega_1)$.
The exit of an ideal evaporative cooler is at the adiabatic saturation (wet-bulb) temperature.

questions.stem: Which describes the air leaving a cooling coil that is dehumidifying the supply air?

options.text: It is at a lower temperature and an unchanged humidity ratio
It is at a higher humidity ratio
It is at a lower temperature and a lower humidity ratio, and close to saturation
It is at the same temperature but at a lower humidity ratio

questions.correctOptionText: It is at a lower temperature and a lower humidity ratio, and close to saturation

distractorRationale.a: The humidity ratio is unchanged only when the coil surface is above the dew point.
distractorRationale.d: The coil cools the air as well as dries it.

questions.explanation: Air is cooled below its dew point, so vapour condenses and $\omega$ falls. The air leaves close to saturation at about the coil-surface temperature.

questions.stem: On the psychrometric chart, where does the state of an adiabatic mixture of two moist-air streams lie?

options.text: On the straight line joining the two inlet states, closer to the stream with the larger dry-air mass flow
On the saturation curve between the two states
Above the state with the higher humidity ratio
At the average of the two relative humidities

questions.correctOptionText: On the straight line joining the two inlet states, closer to the stream with the larger dry-air mass flow

distractorRationale.b: Mixing does not generally saturate the air.
distractorRationale.c: The mixture lies between the two, not beyond.
distractorRationale.d: Relative humidity is not conserved in mixing.

questions.explanation: Since both $\omega$ and $h$ mix as mass-flow-weighted averages, the mixed state lies on the chord connecting states 1 and 2. Its distances from the two end states are in inverse proportion to the dry-air flows.

questions.stem: Dry air passes through an ideal evaporative cooler (adiabatic, with water added). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The dry-bulb temperature rises and the humidity ratio falls
The dry-bulb temperature falls and the humidity ratio is unchanged
The enthalpy falls strongly because of the cooling
The dry-bulb temperature falls and the humidity ratio rises, with enthalpy nearly unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: The dry-bulb temperature falls and the humidity ratio rises, with enthalpy nearly unchanged

distractorRationale.a: This is the opposite of evaporative cooling.
distractorRationale.c: The latent heat for evaporation comes from the air's own sensible heat, so $h$ is about constant.

questions.explanation: The energy needed to evaporate water comes from sensible heat of the air, so $T$ falls while the vapour content rises. Since no heat crosses the boundary, $h$ is essentially constant.

questions.stem: An engineer computes the load of a cooling coil by $\dot m_a c_p (T_1 - T_2)$ only. For air that is dehumidified by the coil, the calculation is

options.text: an overestimate, because the vapour adds to the enthalpy
an underestimate, because the latent load due to condensation of vapour is omitted
exact, because the humidity does not affect the enthalpy
exact, provided $c_p$ is taken at the mean temperature

questions.correctOptionText: an underestimate, because the latent load due to condensation of vapour is omitted

distractorRationale.a: Omitting the vapour condensation term understates the load.
distractorRationale.c: Vapour carries a large latent enthalpy.
distractorRationale.d: The latent term is separate from $c_p$.

questions.explanation: Condensing vapour releases latent heat of about 2450 kJ/kg, which the coil must absorb in addition to the sensible heat. The correct load uses the enthalpy difference of the moist air.

questions.stem: Two moist-air streams are mixed adiabatically. Stream A has a dry-air mass flow of 4 kg/s and stream B has 1 kg/s. What is the correct way to find the mixture's humidity ratio?

options.text: Take the simple average of the two humidity ratios
Weight them by the volume flow rates of the streams
Weight the humidity ratios by the dry-air mass flows, $(4\omega_A + 1\omega_B)/5$
Weight them by the relative humidities of the streams

questions.correctOptionText: Weight the humidity ratios by the dry-air mass flows, $(4\omega_A + 1\omega_B)/5$

distractorRationale.b: Densities differ, so volume weighting is wrong.
distractorRationale.d: Relative humidity is not a conserved quantity.

questions.explanation: Water mass is conserved, so $\dot m_{a3}\omega_3 = \dot m_{a1}\omega_1 + \dot m_{a2}\omega_2$. The dry-air mass flow is the quantity that is conserved and used as the weight.

questions.stem: Air flows at 0.80 kg/s (dry air) through an evaporative humidifier, and its humidity ratio rises from 0.0075 to 0.0118 kg/kg dry air. How much water is added in kg/h?
questions.explanation: Water added $= \dot m_a(\omega_2 - \omega_1) = 0.80\times0.0043 = 0.00344$ kg/s. Multiplying by 3600 s/h gives 12.38 kg/h.

questions.stem: Stream A of 1.2 kg/s dry air with enthalpy 72.0 kJ/kg dry air mixes adiabatically with stream B of 0.80 kg/s dry air with enthalpy 38.0 kJ/kg dry air. Calculate the enthalpy of the mixture in kJ/kg dry air.
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved, so $h_3 = (1.2\times72.0 + 0.8\times38.0)/2.0$. Hence $h_3 = (86.4 + 30.4)/2.0 = 58.40$ kJ/kg dry air.

questions.stem: Air at 1.5 kg/s (dry air) enters a cooling coil with $h_1 = 68.0$ kJ/kg and $\omega_1 = 0.0150$, and leaves with $h_2 = 36.0$ kJ/kg and $\omega_2 = 0.0085$. The condensate leaves at 11 °C with $h_f = 46.2$ kJ/kg. Calculate the cooling load in kW.
Explain why an air-conditioning coil must cool the air below its dew point to dehumidify it, and describe how the cooling load is divided into sensible and latent parts.
markingGuide: Dew point is the temperature at which vapour begins to condense at constant $\omega$
If the coil surface is above the dew point no condensation occurs and $\omega$ stays constant
Below the dew point vapour condenses on the cold surface so $\omega$ falls
The air leaves near saturation at a temperature close to the coil surface temperature
Sensible load is the heat to lower the dry-bulb temperature
Latent load is the heat removed by condensing vapour (about 2450 kJ/kg of water)
Total load from the enthalpy difference, plus a small condensate enthalpy term
questions.explanation: Dehumidification needs the air to touch a surface colder than its dew point, so water condenses. The load is the sum of the sensible heat to cool the air and the latent heat released by the condensing vapour.

questions.stem: A designer proposes an evaporative cooler for two sites. Site A: air at 35 °C with $\omega = 0.0100$ (dry climate). Site B: air at 35 °C with $\omega = 0.0220$ (humid climate). For an ideal cooler leaving saturated, the adiabatic saturation temperature is about 21 °C at site A and about 28 to 29 °C at site B. Use the enthalpy of the inlet air to explain why, estimate the water added at site A for 1.0 kg/s of dry air, and state which site is suitable.
markingGuide: Ideal evaporative cooler follows a line of constant enthalpy to the saturation curve
Higher moisture content at B means a higher wet-bulb temperature because the saturated air on that constant-$h$ line is at a higher temperature
So the temperature drop is about 14 K at A but only about 6 to 7 K at B
Water added at A $= 1.0\times(0.0156 - 0.0100) = 0.0056$ kg/s (about 20 kg/h)
Site A is suitable; evaporative cooling needs dry air with a low wet-bulb temperature
Adds that the supply air becomes more humid, which can affect comfort
questions.explanation: At constant enthalpy the achievable temperature is the wet-bulb temperature, which is much higher in humid air. At the dry site the air cools by 14 K using 0.0056 kg of water per kg of dry air; at the humid site the cooling is small, so the dry site is the suitable one.
